title: Sampling Distributions for the Difference Between Two Sample Means
videoTitle: AP Statistics Topic 4.6 Sampling Distributions for the Difference Between Two Sample Means
intro: Describe the sampling distribution of a difference of independent means and interpret probabilities with a consistent subtraction order.

moments.title: Define the order
moments.text: Keep population 1 minus population 2 throughout the analysis.

moments.title: Center of differences
moments.text: The center is the difference of population means.

moments.title: Add variance contributions
moments.text: Independent variability combines by adding variances, even for a difference.

moments.title: Sampling independence
moments.text: Check each sampling fraction against its own population.

moments.title: Shape of the difference
moments.text: Both mean distributions must support the normal model.

moments.title: Independent groups
moments.text: Two-sample formulas require independence between groups.

moments.title: Commute times
moments.text: Compare average commutes in two metropolitan areas.

moments.title: Which average is larger?
moments.text: A difference below zero means the first sample mean is smaller.

cards.name: Order
cards.text: Define A minus B; a positive difference means A is larger.

cards.name: Conditions
cards.text: Use independent random samples, check each 10% condition when sampling without replacement, and justify approximately normal mean distributions for both groups.

questions.obj: Find the probability one sample mean is smaller
questions.q: In the video, metro A has population mean commute 34 minutes, SD 10 minutes, and sample size 50. Metro B has mean 29, SD 12, and sample size 70. The random samples are independent. Assume at least 500 people in A and 700 in B and no extreme population skewness. Find the probability that A's sample mean is smaller than B's.

steps.t: Define the difference and check conditions.

work.text: Let D be sample mean A minus sample mean B. The samples are independent and random, fractions are at most 10%, and both sample sizes exceed 30.
Subtract means, but add variance contributions.
A smaller first mean is the event D<0.
Use the normal model for D.

questions.answer: About 0.65% of such independent pairs of samples have a smaller sample mean commute in A despite A's higher population mean.

sections.title: Calculate a probability for a difference
sections.intro: Start with the empty calculator. Type each expression yourself; a video link reviews the underlying method.

steps.title: Combine sampling variability
steps.suppose: we want the SD of A minus B.
steps.observe: The plus sign combines independent variance contributions.

steps.title: Find the probability
steps.suppose: we want the first sample mean to be smaller.
steps.observe: The event is a negative A-minus-B difference.

traps.title: Subtracting variability
traps.better: For independent sample means, add the variance contributions and then take a square root.

traps.title: Reversing the event
traps.weak: A below B means A minus B is positive.
traps.better: A below B means A minus B is negative.

traps.title: One large sample is enough
traps.weak: The difference is normal whenever either sample is large.
traps.better: Justify a normal model for both component sample means.

traps.title: Wrong population denominator
traps.weak: Compare the total sample size with one population.
traps.better: Check each sample size against its respective population size.

questions.stem: Independent population SDs are 12 and 8, with sample sizes 36 and 16. What is the SD of the difference of sample means?
why: The two independent variance contributions are 4 and 4.
The SDs must be squared and the total square-rooted.
This omits sample sizes and subtracts variances.

questions.stem: Population means are 40 and 35. The center of sample mean A minus sample mean B is:
why: Means are subtracted for this difference.
The expected difference equals the population mean difference.

questions.stem: Which situation requires a paired method instead of an independent two-sample method?
opts: The same people measured before and after training
Unrelated randomly sampled products from two factories
why: Measurements within a person are paired.
Different independent experimental units support a two-group comparison.

questions.stem: If D is defined as A minus B, what does D>3 mean?
opts: B exceeds A by more than 3
A and B are both above 3
A exceeds B by more than 3
why: D is a difference, not A alone.
Both values can be below 3 while their difference exceeds 3.
This translates the defined difference correctly.

sections.title: Write a complete response
sections.prompt: Two independent normal populations of component lengths have means 102 and 100 mm, with SDs 6 and 8 mm. Independent random samples contain 36 and 64 components from populations exceeding 10,000 each.
parts: (a) Describe the distribution of sample mean A minus sample mean B and verify conditions.
(b) Calculate the probability that A's sample mean is below B's.
(c) Explain the effect of quadrupling both sample sizes.
sample: (a) Both samples are independent and random, sampling fractions are below 10%, and the populations are normal. The difference is normal with mean 2 mm and SD √(36/36+64/64)=√2 mm.
(b) The event is D<0. Its z-score is (0−2)/√2≈-1.4142, giving probability 0.0786.
(c) The center stays 2 mm. Both variance contributions divide by four, so the sampling SD is halved. The chance that the first mean is below the second becomes smaller.
checklist: Checks independent random sampling and sampling fractions.
Gives the correct center and sampling SD.
Translates the event and calculates its probability.
Explains the effect of larger sample sizes.
